newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa unions begin protests over new labour law.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa unions begin protests over new labour law.

text.p: South Africa's largest trade union federation started a week of protests on Monday over proposed employment legislation as business called for continuing negotiations.
The 1.9-million member Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) plans 24-hour strikes in each of the country's nine provinces from Monday to Thursday this week.
Labour and business are at loggerheads over issues such as a reduced working week, maternity leave and overtime rates.
The federation said it was not yet able to estimate support for the first day's strike, in the Eastern Cape region, because workers were not scheduled to join protest marches until later in the day.
Business South Africa negotiator Adrian du Plessis told state radio that mass action would not end the impasse in talks over the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill.
"The issues are very difficult and I must confess the parties are deeply divided," he said.
"But the proposed programme of protest action has not helped in bringing the parties together at all. If anything it has hardened the attitudes on both sides of the table rather than softened them."
Cosatu wants six months' maternity leave, four with pay, and a 40-hour working week within five years.

Business has agreed to reduce the working week by an hour to 45 hours, but refuses to commit to a 40-hour week. It argues that some of the bill's provisions could raise employment costs to the point of deterring job creation.
Cosatu spokeswoman Noweto Mpati told Reuters no new proposals had been made by Monday and there was no reason to resume already prolonged talks with business.
"We don't have time to waste as Cosatu. We would like this bill to go to parliament this year," she said.

Labour Minister Tito Mboweni has warned repeatedly that the bill would not become law this year unless broad consensus could be reached between business and labour in time for its presentation to parliament on September 15.
Du Plessis said strike action contradicted the foundation of the country's new industrial relations system, based on resolving conflicts through negotiation.

"Protest action divides the parties and in the end it's destructive to the economy. It doesn't bring us together -- it drives us apart. To that extent I think it's extremely damaging, notwithstanding what it does to local and investor confidence."
